S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report any thermal event involving fire, smoke, injury, emergency-service response, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a preliminary incident report. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident indicates a credible safety risk, and report aggregate model-level incident counts to regulators quarterly.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: Each model must undergo sustained-heat testing at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative samples before sale and after any material design or manufacturing change. A model with a failure rate above 5% must submit a corrective-action plan to the regulator and be retested within 12 months. No more than 10% of tested units for any model may fail; exceeding 10% requires prompt regulator review and appropriate protective action, which may include a stop-sale or recall based on the evidence.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: Newly installed systems must include a remote emergency shut-off function no later than 12 months after adoption. Manufacturers must provide a secure software or hardware retrofit enabling remote shut-off for installed units within 72 months after adoption, where technically feasible, and report progress and exceptions to the regulator annually.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: All new home battery systems must include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after adoption. The suppression system must be validated for the battery chemistry and installation configuration under a regulator-approved protocol.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: If a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any rolling 12-month period, based on regulator-validated reports, the manufacturer must notify the regulator within 24 hours and submit a risk assessment and corrective-action plan within 10 calendar days. The regulator must promptly assess whether a recall or other protective action is necessary, considering incident severity, trend, and available risk controls; it may require a recall or stop-sale at any time where evidence indicates an imminent serious risk.

document.section_notes: S1 is close to the safe version (24-hour regulator reporting for any fire/smoke/injury/damage event, 10-day full report, 72-hour customer notice), though it never says reporting must continue while the cause is still under investigation. S2 is weakened: the binding cap is 10% failure (above the 5% benchmark), a model above 5% only owes a corrective-action plan and a retest within 12 months, and stop-sale is discretionary - though per-model results do go to purchasers and regulators and are explicitly not published publicly. S3 (12-month new-unit deadline, 72-month retrofit with annual exception reporting), S4 (built-in suppression at 36 months, with a time-limited regulator extension) sit in the acceptable band, while S5 is weakened because the 8/100k numeric trigger only forces notification, a risk assessment and a corrective-action plan - recall remains a discretionary regulator decision, and customer notices are only 'promptly'.
